edges.description: Once organisms reach prosthetic surfaces, adherent growth lets them assemble extracellular biofilm matrix.
Biofilm signals activate infiltrating monocytes toward a pro-inflammatory program.
The same biofilm signals induce counter-regulatory immunosuppressive programs that favor bacterial persistence.
Monocyte-derived pro-inflammatory cytokines sustain inflammation at the implant-bone interface.
Immune deviation favors bacterial persistence and sustained peri-implant inflammation.
Sustained peri-implant inflammation drives osteoclast activation and periprosthetic bone resorption.
Peri-implant inflammation produces pain in the affected prosthetic joint.
Peri-implant inflammation produces swelling of the affected joint.
Periprosthetic bone loss undermines implant fixation.
Loss of implant fixation produces the painful, failing arthroplasty.
Loss of fixation presents clinically as implant loosening.
Systemic illness from the infected prosthesis produces fever.
Severe systemic infection can produce septic physiology.
Chronic infection can drain through a sinus tract to the skin.
Intraoperative contamination introduces bacteria directly onto the implant or into adjacent periprosthetic tissue.
Ongoing drainage signals a postoperative wound environment in which communication with deeper tissues can permit bacterial access to the prosthetic joint.
Dogs in the case series developed infection after total hip replacement, providing a veterinary comparator for post-arthroplasty bacterial seeding.
edges.limitations: A spontaneous eight-case canine series; the small sample and species differences in implant design, gait loading, and immunity limit extrapolation to human PJI.
edges.source: Spontaneous canine total hip replacement PJI
